title: Are microplastics harming us?
intro: How much plastic do you use on a daily basis? And how much of it is used to package or prepare food? Recently, scientists are becoming increasingly concerned that microplastics, tiny bits of plastic invisible to the naked eye, are entering our bodies through these food sources... but it is unclear exactly what the long-term health effects will be. Becca and Phil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
this_week_question: How long would it take to ingest a credit-card-sized amount of microplastics?
a) 13,000 years b) 23,000 years c) 33,000 years
Listen to the programme to hear the answer.

vocab.desc: related to, found in or produced by the sea emerging coming into view after being hidden, allowing a better understanding or development correlation relationship between two or more things spike sudden, sharp increase in something quantified measured and given a number or a value exposure come into contact with something that may have an impact on you

transcript.text: So, my question for you is how long would it really take to ingest that amount of microplastics? Would it be: a)    13,000 years, b)    23,000 years, or c)    33,000 years?

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: Well, I want to be hopeful, so I'll go with the longest period of time. That would be 33,000 years.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: OK. Well, we'll find out the answer at the end of the programme.

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: So, the World Health Organisation says that microplastics have been found in many different food groups. But Phil, what is the food group that is more affected by microplastics?

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Well, scientists have found that seafood is one of the main food groups where microplastics can be found, and BBC World Service programme The Evidence has been investigating this. Professor Shilpa Chokshi told host Claudia Hammond about some pictures that she was shown by a microplastics expert.

transcript.author: Professor Shilpa Chokshi
transcript.text: And he showed me all these marine animals that looked like they had plastics in their livers and hind guts. And from that initial discussion, I went away and I looked at the literature and I looked at the data, and there was emerging evidence that there was plastics in the liver, and there was this correlation increase.

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: Shilpa says that plastics have been found in marine animals. Marine describes anything related to, found in or produced by the sea.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Yes, these pictures of marine animals with plastics in their bodies inspired Shilpa to dive deeper into the data. She found emerging evidence, and the adjective emerging describes something coming into view after being hidden, allowing it to develop or be better understood.

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: And from this emerging evidence, Shilpa noticed a correlation . You'll hear this word a lot when talking about data. A correlation is a link or connection between two or more things. So, Phil, we know how toxic microplastics get into our body, but are they definitely harmful?

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Well, plastics have been a big part of daily life since the 1950s, but it's only recently that we've started thinking about microplastics as a health issue. For example, scientists have been looking at people who worked in nylon factories where they were exposed to high levels of microplastic. And the scientists think that there may be a correlation between this and diseases that they developed later on. Science professor Mark Miodownik, from University College London, has mixed feelings about microplastics and explained these to BBC World Service programme The Evidence.

transcript.author: Professor Mark Miodownik
transcript.text: Well, you know, we have been exposed for decades and surely if it was that bad, you know, we'd have seen a spike or something by now. But on the other hand, you know, I think, you know, if you look at how much plastic packaging is in supermarkets, it's gone up and up and up and up. And this is not a quantified measure, but our exposure seems to be increasing, and that's the worry for me.

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: Mark mentions that some people say if microplastics were harmful, we surely would have seen a spike in issues related to them by now. A spike is literally a pointy shape, but here it means a sudden, sharp increase in something.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Right. And though the amount of plastic packaging we use has increased, this isn't a quantified measure. If something is quantified , then it's measured and given a number or a value.

transcript.author: Becca
transcript.text: So, Mark concludes that he is worried about our exposure to plastics. Exposure means coming into contact with something that may have an impact on you. OK. Phil, so, if people are worried about their exposure to microplastics, what can they do to reduce this?

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Well, one thing they can do is to replace things like plastic chopping boards, utensils and food storage containers. And another tip from BBC World Service's The Evidence is to replace tea bags, which often contain microplastics, with loose-leaf tea. OK. Becca, now it's time to get the answer to our quiz question.
